title: A Preregistered Audit of Dataset Contamination Controls in LLM-for-NetOps Benchmarks
abstract: We preregistered and executed a paired confirmatory audit to evaluate conservative deterministic contamination detectors (exact normalized token equality; fuzzy 5‑gram overlap; provenance heuristics) and a guarded exclusion policy on a reproducible 150‑item NetOps sample. The preregistered design (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) used one hosted model (gpt-5-mini) and a deterministic NetOps verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5). Execution produced no preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags; because the run used provenance‑stable synthetic items and shared_initial_candidate generation semantics, a single shared generation per item was reused for baseline and guarded conditions (model_calls_used = 150). All validator episodes passed (baseline = 150/150; guarded = 150/150). The paired success‑rate difference = 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]); exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. We reconcile the preregistration and execution artifacts to explain why this outcome is degenerate for detecting generation‑level contamination, document execution accounting (planned_episode_count = 300; completed_episode_count = 300; failed_episode_count = 0), and give artifact‑grounded recommendations—provenance‑rich sampling, independent per‑condition generation, multi‑model scope, per‑item overlap logging, and paraphrase‑robust detectors—to increase audit sensitivity in future work.

sections.introduction:
LLMs are increasingly proposed for NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation and automated configuration repair. Reliable operational adoption requires benchmark evidence that reflects real capability rather than dataset leakage or templating artifacts that confound apparent accuracy. Prior surveys and benchmark studies emphasize two recurring risks: contamination of benchmark items by model training data and construct invalidity from overly templated prompts.

This paper reports a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored confirmatory audit (study_id = contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1) that asked: under conservative deterministic detectors and a conservative guarded exclusion policy, how many high‑confidence contamination flags occur in a reproducible 150‑item sample, and how much does applying those controls change an LLM's validator pass rate? Our principal contributions are: (1) a preregistered paired design executed end‑to‑end with archived artifacts and deterministic validator traces; (2) exact, artifact‑verified confirmatory statistics (complete_pair_count = 150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0; guarded_success_rate = 1.0; paired difference = 0.0; CI = [0.0,0.0]; McNemar p = 1.0); and (3) an explicit preregistration→execution reconciliation that explains why the run produced a degenerate null result and provides concrete, artifact‑grounded design changes to increase audit sensitivity.

Crucially, and stated up front: the executed confirmatory sample consisted of provenance‑stable synthetic tasks generated by the preregistered deterministic task generator, and the run used shared_initial_candidate (independent_condition_generation = false) semantics so that, in the absence of high‑confidence flags, the same model generation served both baseline and guarded episodes. Those execution facts—recorded in the archived execution bundle—limit the inferential scope: the observed zero‑flag, zero‑difference outcome pertains to this synthetic, shared‑generation regime and does not imply absence of contamination in independent public benchmarks or across other LLMs.
sections.related_work:
Work on LLM‑driven NetOps demonstrates that language models can synthesize device configurations or repair suggestions under constrained conditions and that combining LLMs with verifiers or iterative validate–repair loops improves average reliability compared to naive generation. System papers (e.g., automatic‑repair efforts and agentic repair evaluations) report promising results but also document per‑case regressions and sensitivity to dataset design and tooling.

Formal network verification methods (Header Space Analysis and related verification frameworks) are practical oracles for reachability and policy checks and are used as validators in produce–validate pipelines; these tools motivated our choice of a deterministic NetOps validator as the scoring oracle. Separately, surveys and meta‑analyses of LLM evaluation highlight contamination and construct validity as major threats to correct interpretation of benchmarked accuracy. This literature motivated our preregistered conservative detectors (exact equality, fuzzy 5‑gram overlap thresholds, provenance timestamp heuristics) and the guarded exclusion policy for high‑confidence flags.

Positioning. Unlike broad capability benchmarks, our study is a methodological audit: we test whether a prespecified conservative set of contamination controls would change validator‑measured success in a reproducible sample under the archived execution semantics. The nearest prior work calls for contamination‑aware benchmarks and richer provenance; our contribution is an executed preregistration and an artifact‑grounded reconciliation that identifies concrete design levers auditors must control to achieve sensitivity.
sections.methodology:
Preregistration and estimands. The study preregistered a paired binary design with primary estimand paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline. The preregistered analysis executor (paired_binary_analysis_v1) runs an exact McNemar two‑sided test and computes a paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, fixed seed) for the paired difference.

Detectors and guarded policy (preregistered). The preregistered detectors were: (1) exact normalized token equality after canonicalization; (2) fuzzy 5‑gram shingle overlap (Jaccard/overlap) with planned high‑confidence threshold ≥ 0.80 and sensitivity checks at 0.65 and 0.50; and (3) provenance timestamp heuristics comparing item timestamps to model cutoff. The guarded policy deterministically excluded only high‑confidence flagged items (exact match OR fuzzy overlap ≥ 0.80) and replaced them with deterministic retemplated topology‑augmented alternatives sampled from the same generator distribution with fixed seeds; replacements required embedding similarity to preserve intent.

Sampling, generation semantics, and execution contract. The preregistration allowed deterministic task generation for reproducibility. The executed run used a deterministic_netops_task_generator (synthetic item identifiers) and set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate). Under this semantics, when no high‑confidence flags occurred a single model generation per item satisfied both baseline and guarded episodes. The preregistration also specified maximum_model_calls = 300 and a planned_episode_count = 300 (150 items × 2 conditions). The execution bundle records that model_calls_used = 150 because shared generation removed the need for separate per‑condition calls when no exclusions triggered.

Verification oracle and scoring. We used a deterministic NetOps verifier (deterministic_netops_validator_v5) implementing parse→state update→property checks and returning both a binary pass/fail score and structured validator traces (e.g., parsed_command_count, observed_touched_field_count, final_state). The scoring rule for intent→configuration tasks required that generated configurations produce the intended final state and respect workflow policies (full_intent_constraint_validation).

Planned analyses and sensitivities. The primary confirmatory test was prespecified. Sensitivity analyses included treating failed model calls as failures, evaluating alternative fuzzy thresholds (0.50, 0.65, 0.80), and stratifying by templated vs realistic items. The preregistration included power guidance showing that single‑model single‑call designs have reduced sensitivity compared to multi‑model plans; we report this tradeoff explicitly in the Discussion.
sections.results:
Execution accounting and deterministic reconciliation. Execution completed planned_episode_count = 300 (150 items × 2 conditions) with completed_episode_count = 300 and failed_episode_count = 0. Deterministic reconciliation confirms complete_pair_count = 150. Provider‑call auditing shows hosted_model_call_event_count = 150 (no failed calls), cache_miss_count = 150, and no cross‑condition cache reuse that would invalidate accounting under the shared_initial semantics.

Contamination detector outcome. The preregistered detectors produced zero high‑confidence contamination flags for the executed sample. The contamination_summary artifact contains no flagged rows. Importantly, the detector pipeline in this execution recorded explicit per‑item fuzzy overlap outputs only for episodes that met the preregistered flagging criteria or required replacement operations; because no episodes reached the high‑confidence threshold, the archived detector logs do not contain an aggregated distribution of per‑item overlap scores to report. We therefore report the documented absence of preregistered high‑confidence flags rather than inventing overlap‑distribution statistics.

Validator outcomes and confirmatory statistics. The deterministic_netops_validator_v5 returned pass for all baseline episodes (baseline_success_count = 150/150; baseline_success_rate = 1.0) and all guarded episodes (guarded_success_count = 150/150; guarded_success_rate = 1.0). The paired contingency table is n11 = 150, n10 = 0, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. The primary estimand (guarded − baseline) = 0.0 percentage points. Paired bootstrap percentile 95% CI (10,000 resamples, seed fixed) = [0.0, 0.0]. Exact McNemar two‑sided p = 1.0. All per‑episode raw responses and validator traces are archived in the execution bundle.

Representative exemplar. A representative archived episode (task-000001) demonstrates the artifact structure and validator trace: normalized_response = "interface edge1 admin down\ninterface edge1 vlan 30\ninterface edge1 mtu 1600\ninterface edge1 admin up"; the validator returned score = 1 with parsed_command_count = 4 and final_state matching the intent. This exemplar is representative of the 150 successful pairs and illustrates the canonicalized normalization and verifier checks used to produce binary scoring.

What the numerical outcome means. The observed zero difference is an artifact‑supported fact for this execution regime: provenance‑stable synthetic items and shared generation semantics led to identical baseline and guarded outputs per item when no high‑confidence flags were found. Consequently, the paired test had no discordant pairs to inform a difference estimate. The numerical results are thus internally consistent and replicate across the archived bootstrap resampling, but they do not imply that the preregistered detectors would fail to flag contamination in web‑sourced benchmarks or under independent per‑condition generation.
sections.discussion:
Why the null is degenerate (artifact‑grounded explanation). Two archived facts explain the degenerate result. First, the confirmatory sample was generated deterministically from a synthetic task generator; such items are unlikely to exact‑match or strongly overlap with public corpus fingerprints used by fuzzy detectors. Second, execution set independent_condition_generation = false (shared_initial_candidate), so baseline and guarded episodes re‑used a single model generation per item when no exclusion occurred. Together these facts mechanistically produced identical baseline and guarded outputs per item and therefore made the paired comparison uninformative for generation‑level contamination detection in this run. Both facts and provider accounting are recorded in the execution bundle and deterministic reconciliation artifacts.

Audit sensitivity and design tradeoffs. The preregistered power guidance shows that a single‑model, shared‑generation design reduces detectable paired differences compared to multi‑model, independent re‑generation designs. In practice, auditors aiming to detect leakage in web‑sourced benchmarks should (a) sample provenance‑rich public items, (b) set independent_condition_generation = true (independent model calls per condition), and (c) expand to multiple models and independent seeds to amplify discordant signals. The archived run demonstrates reproducible execution mechanics but also highlights that preregistered flexibility (allowing deterministic generators and shared generation) can, when chosen, reduce audit sensitivity; auditors should make these tradeoffs explicit when designing audits.

Operational implications for NetOps evaluation. For practitioners using LLMs in NetOps, the run shows two practical points. First, deterministic, validator‑backed scoring can reliably check functional constraints and produce detailed execution traces suitable for forensic auditing. Second, contamination audits intended to assess public benchmark leakage must avoid provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and must force independent generation per condition. Validator success alone (as in this run) indicates correctness with respect to the verifier's modeled properties but not comprehensive production readiness.

Recommendations grounded in artifacts. Based on the preregistration and archived execution, we recommend auditors: (1) use provenance‑rich, web‑sourced samples when the goal is detecting training‑data leakage; (2) log per‑item fuzzy overlap scores regardless of thresholded flags so post‑hoc distributions are available even when flags are rare; (3) use independent per‑condition generations to avoid shared‑output collapse; (4) expand to multiple models and seeds to detect cross‑model leakage signals; and (5) add paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication for borderline cases. Each recommendation follows directly from the execution bundle's recorded semantics and from the empty contamination_summary artifact observed here.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered, artifact‑anchored paired audit of conservative contamination detectors on a reproducible 150‑item synthetic NetOps sample. Execution produced zero preregistered high‑confidence contamination flags and identical validator pass rates (150/150 baseline, 150/150 guarded); the paired difference estimate is 0.0 percentage points (95% CI [0.0, 0.0]; McNemar p = 1.0). The degenerate null outcome is artifact‑supported and stems from provenance‑stable synthetic sampling and shared generation semantics, which together eliminated discordant pairs in the paired design. We do not generalize this null to web‑sourced benchmarks. The archived execution artifacts document provider accounting, validator traces, and the empty contamination summary; they motivate concrete design changes for audits that seek sensitivity to real‑world leakage. All experiment artifacts and traces are archived in the execution bundle and available for verification as described in the Disclosure Statement below.

disclosure_statement: This study was executed under the autonomous preregistration contamination-audit-netops-2026-v1. LLM used: gpt-5-mini. Orchestration adapter: hosted_netops_gvr_v1. Deterministic task generator and validator used as executables in the run (generator and validator version identifiers archived in the execution bundle). The exact immutable initial master‑prompt reference is archived at provenance/master_prompt.txt (SHA‑256: 1872df1e1805d2d96940456ca016bd665d1d5196add77f5acdf1582bb39b15ba). Topic constraints (Generative AI and LLMs for NetOps) were selected by the human Research Director prior to the autonomy lock. After the autonomy lock, the AI autonomously performed literature search, gap selection, preregistration, experiment execution, analysis, manuscript drafting, AI peer review, and revision. All generation prompts, model outputs, validator traces, sampling seeds, execution logs, and analysis artifacts were produced and archived by the autonomous pipeline and are included in the execution bundle. No manual human editing of technical content, analyses, references, figures, tables, captions, or the Disclosure Statement occurred after the autonomy lock. Pre‑lock development and rehearsal runs occurred but were not used as empirical evidence unless re‑created under the locked pipeline. The execution followed preregistered missingness, retry, and exclusion policies; no deviations from the preregistration that affect the primary estimand occurred.
limitations: Single‑model execution (gpt‑5-mini) — results do not generalize across other LLM families, sizes, or proprietary training corpora.

Sampled items were provenance‑stable synthetic tasks (generator produced items with synthetic identifiers) for this run; absence of high‑confidence flags here may not reflect contamination prevalence in web‑crawled public benchmarks.

Generation semantics used shared_initial_candidate across baseline and guarded conditions (independent_condition_generation = false). When no exclusions occurred this produced identical model outputs for paired episodes, limiting the paired test's sensitivity to generation‑level contamination.

Contamination detection relied on preregistered conservative heuristics (exact match and fuzzy 5‑gram overlap); subtler contamination patterns (paraphrased memorization) may escape these heuristics and require paraphrase‑robust detectors and human adjudication.

Passing the deterministic_netops_validator_v5 indicates satisfaction of checked functional constraints but does not imply production readiness or absence of semantic regressions outside the validator's modeled properties.
